Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 50
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: South Asian
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Diplomat
  trauma_type: Toxic chemical exposure
  pcl5: 34

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Stressors: avoid anything that could be stressful, Magical Thinking: I tell myself the event did not really happen or was not that bad, Avoid Thinking: Thinking about the event
  Threat: Irritability: Irritable behavior, angry outbursts, or acting aggressively, Body on Alert: My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger, Scanning for Danger: I constantly scan my surroundings for signs of danger
  Memory: Triggered Without Warning: Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning, Cannot Explain Clearly: When I try to explain what happened I lose the thread and cannot finish, Taste Vividness: I can taste what I tasted during the event when the memory returns

Vignette:
Meera had spent twenty years navigating the delicate architecture of international agreements, her days a careful choreography of handshakes, translated documents, and the precise language of diplomacy. She was known for her composure. So when the delegation from the industrial consortium arrived at the consulate in Geneva that Tuesday morning, she greeted them with her usual calm, offering coffee and mineral water before they began the afternoon’s negotiations. It was during the second hour of the meeting that she first noticed the faint, acrid smell—something like burnt plastic and sulphur, seeping from a vent above the conference table. She mentioned it to a colleague, who shrugged. No one else seemed alarmed. By the third hour, the taste had settled on her tongue, metallic and greasy, and her eyes were watering. She excused herself, walked to the restroom, and vomited into the sink. She spent the night in a clinic, her throat raw, her skin prickling, the doctors saying it was a minor leak, nothing critical, she would be fine. But the taste never truly left her.

In the weeks that followed, Meera found herself unable to sit in any enclosed room without her neck prickling. She stopped attending briefings in the conference room, claiming a scheduling conflict. She began eating lunch at her desk, alone, because the consulate cafeteria had a similar recycled air quality that made her stomach turn. What frightened her most, though, was the way the memory could ambush her. She would be walking down a corridor, or standing at a crosswalk, and the taste would flood her mouth without warning—sulphur and burnt plastic—and she would be back in that room, her throat closing, the world gone grey. She had no time to brace herself. And when people asked what happened, when a colleague pressed her for details about the leak, she would open her mouth and find the words had scattered. She could not hold the thread of the story. She would say, “There was a smell,” and then stop, the sentence dissolving into silence.

She began to tell herself, with increasing conviction, that it had not really been that bad. The doctors had said she was fine. Perhaps she had overreacted. Perhaps it was all in her head. This thought offered a strange, temporary relief, and she would repeat it like a mantra: it wasn’t that bad, it didn’t really happen, you imagined it. But her body did not believe her. She was constantly tense, her shoulders locked, her jaw tight, as if waiting for a blow. She scanned every room she entered—the ceiling vents, the gaps under doors, the faces of strangers who might be carrying something invisible. Her irritability grew. A junior staff member’s innocent question about a filing deadline would make her snap, her voice sharp and cruel, and she would see the hurt in their eyes and feel a distant shame, but the anger was already there, hot and ready.

The avoidance spread like a slow stain. She stopped accepting invitations to dinners or receptions, because crowds were unpredictable and someone might be wearing strong perfume, or the kitchen might have a gas stove, and the stress of managing that possibility was too much. She cancelled a bilateral meeting in a hotel, claiming illness, because she could not bear the thought of an unfamiliar ventilation system. Her supervisor noticed. A quiet conversation was had about her recent performance, her absences from key sessions. Meera nodded, promised to do better, and then went home and sat in the dark, her body still tense, her mouth dry, tasting nothing.

What finally brought her to seek help was a morning in the consulate garden. She was standing alone, watching a gardener trim a hedge, and she realised she was calculating the wind direction. She was checking whether the smell of cut leaves could carry anything toxic. She was, she understood with a hollow clarity, never not scanning. She was exhausted. She made the appointment that afternoon, not because she believed talking would help, but because she was afraid of what she might become if she did not. She was most afraid, she told the therapist, that she would lose her career. That she would be sent home. That the taste would never leave her. And underneath all of that, she was afraid that she was right to be afraid—that the world was, in fact, full of invisible dangers, and that she was the only one paying attention.
